title: Protection against electric shock: fault protection
summary: Explains fault protection: earthing and equipotential bonding, exposed and extraneous conductive parts, automatic disconnection of supply, maximum disconnection times and maximum earth fault loop impedance (Zs).

sections.heading: Recap: protection against electric shock
paragraphs: A person must touch two conductors with a potential greater than 50 Vac for a significant shock. Regulation 410, paragraph 2 states that hazardous-live-parts shall not be accessible and accessible conductive parts shall not be hazardous-live, either in use without a fault or in single fault conditions.
bullets: Basic protection: protection in use without a fault
Fault protection: protection under fault conditions
Combined, they form a protective measure

sections.heading: Earthing and circuit protective conductors
paragraphs: There are two types of protective circuit. Earthing conductors provide a low resistance path, in the event of an earth fault, so a protective device can operate. Equipotential bonding conductors reduce touch voltages during an earth fault. Names of the conductors are listed in BS 7671:2008:A3 Figure 2.1.

BS 7671 defines earthing as the connection of the exposed-conductive parts of an installation to the main earthing terminal of that installation. An earthing conductor is a protective conductor connecting the main earthing terminal to an earth electrode or other means of earthing.
Circuit protective conductors (cpc's) connect all exposed-conductive-parts of equipment to the main earthing terminal (MET).
bullets: Exposed-conductive-part: conductive part of equipment which can be touched, is not normally live, but can become live under fault conditions
Examples: steel conduit, steel trunking, steel tray, metal casing of connected appliances or electronic equipment, the consumer unit enclosure

sections.heading: Equipotential bonding
paragraphs: Protective equipotential bonding is equipotential bonding for the purpose of safety. Equipotential bonding is the electrical connection keeping exposed-conductive-parts and extraneous-conductive-parts at substantially the same potential. The IET On-Site Guide (Section 4.6) says supplementary bonding reduces the voltage between these parts during a fault to earth, creating a zone where such voltages are minimised.

Main protective bonding conductors connect extraneous-conductive-parts of other incoming services and structural metalwork to the main earthing terminal. If the installation meets BS 7671 earthing and bonding requirements, there is no specific requirement for supplementary bonding of certain items.
bullets: Extraneous-conductive-part: a conductive part liable to introduce a potential, generally Earth potential, and not forming part of the electrical installation
Examples: metal water pipes, metal gas pipes, other metal pipework and ducting, central heating and air conditioning systems, exposed metal structural parts

No specific supplementary bonding needed for kitchen pipes, sinks or draining boards, metallic boiler pipework, metal kitchen furniture, metallic pipes to wash-hand basins and WCs, or locations with a bath or shower (if 701.415.2 is met)

sections.heading: Automatic disconnection of supply
paragraphs: The most common measure for fault protection is automatic disconnection of supply: a protective device breaks the supply to a faulty circuit quickly enough that voltages on bonded metalwork cannot persist long enough to cause danger. The maximum times for circuits <32 A are in BS 7671 Chapter 41 and depend on the earthing system and nominal voltage (Uo).

The earth fault current path must have low impedance so the high current needed can flow. If the impedance is too high, fault current is reduced and the device may not operate in time, or at all. Where disconnection cannot be achieved in the required time, supplementary equipotential bonding shall be provided (411.3.2.6).
bullets: Final circuits (Table 41.1): TN system @ < 230 V ac: 0.4 seconds
Final circuits: TT system @ < 230 V ac: 0.2 seconds

sections.heading: Maximum earth fault loop impedance (Zs)
paragraphs: The maximum Zs for the required disconnection time depends on the type of protective device, its current rating (In), the nominal ac voltage to earth (Uo) and the minimum voltage factor (Cmin), taken as 0.95. The expression to be fulfilled is Zs ✕ In < Uo ✕ Cmin.

As the operating current of a device increases, the maximum Zs falls so enough current flows to operate it in time. For example, a BS 88-3 fuse system C rated at 16 A has a maximum Zs of 2.3Ω, while the same type at 32 A has a maximum Zs of 0.91Ω.
bullets: Table 41.3: circuit breakers; 0.4 s; Uo = 230 V
Automatic disconnection involves the cpc, main protective bonding, supplementary bonding, earthing conductor, protective devices and earth electrode (BS 7671 Chapter 41; 411)

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of earthing conductors in a protective circuit?
flashcards.back: They provide a low resistance path, in the event of an earth fault, so a protective device can operate.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of equipotential bonding conductors?
flashcards.back: They reduce touch voltages during an earth fault.
A conductive part of equipment which can be touched and is not normally live, but can become live under fault conditions.
Steel conduit, steel trunking, steel tray, metal casings of connected appliances or electronic equipment, the consumer unit enclosure.
A conductive part liable to introduce a potential, generally Earth potential, and not forming part of the electrical installation.

flashcards.front: What do main protective bonding conductors connect?
flashcards.back: Extraneous-conductive-parts of other incoming services and structural metalwork to the main earthing terminal.

flashcards.front: What is the most common measure for fault protection?
Maximum disconnection time for final circuits on a TN system @ < 230 V ac?
Maximum disconnection time for final circuits on a TT system @ < 230 V ac?
Maximum disconnection times for distribution circuits?
flashcards.back: TN system: 5 seconds (411.3.2.3). TT system: 1 second (411.3.2.4).

flashcards.front: What if automatic disconnection cannot be achieved in the required time?
flashcards.back: Supplementary equipotential bonding shall be provided (411.3.2.6).

flashcards.front: What expression must Zs fulfil, and what is Cmin?
flashcards.back: Zs ✕ In < Uo ✕ Cmin, with the minimum voltage factor Cmin taken to be 0.95.

flashcards.front: What happens to maximum Zs as device rating increases?
flashcards.back: It reduces, so sufficient current flows to operate the device in time. E.g. BS 88-3 fuse system C: 16 A is 2.3Ω, 32 A is 0.91Ω.

quiz.q: What do earthing conductors provide in the event of an earth fault?
options: A low resistance path so a protective device can operate
A means of reducing supply voltage
quiz.why: Earthing conductors give a low resistance path to let a protective device operate.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an exposed-conductive-part?
options: An exposed structural steel beam of the building
quiz.why: Steel conduit is an exposed-conductive-part; the others are extraneous-conductive-parts.

quiz.q: Which is an example of an extraneous-conductive-part?
Where do main protective bonding conductors connect extraneous-conductive-parts?
options: To the cpc at the socket
quiz.why: They connect to the main earthing terminal.

quiz.q: What is the most common measure used for fault protection?
quiz.why: Automatic disconnection of supply is the most common fault protection measure.

quiz.why: The TN final circuit time at < 230 V ac is 0.4 seconds.

quiz.q: What is the maximum disconnection time for a final circuit on a TT system at < 230 V ac?
quiz.why: The TT final circuit time at < 230 V ac is 0.2 seconds.
